source.title: Semantic Alignment of Unimodal Medical Text and Vision Representations
source.authors: Maxime Di Folco; Emily Chan; M. Hasny; Cosmin I. Bercea; J. A. Schnabel

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies semantic alignment and model stitching in a new, specialised medical setting, including cross-modal zero-shot classification.
record.gate_note: The study reports outcomes for anchor-based representation alignment and model stitching, so these are recorded. The methods and model lists it cites are not treated as results. The transformation and anchor-count comparisons are included because the paper explicitly reports their effects.
record.test_reason: The study estimates affine or orthogonal maps from anchors between independently trained text models, between vision models, and from vision to text, all in chest X-ray tasks. It reports how much stitched classification loses against each model's own performance, which bears directly on V4 in a new specialised domain.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that anchor-based semantic alignment transfers medical knowledge without training, beating naive stitching by a large margin and nearly closing the gap for text. Their unimodal zero-shot method beats CLIP on 6 of 7 tasks and is comparable to MedCLIP. The paraphrase should add that medical-to-general stitching loses 10–14%.
record.recipe_differences: Uses anchor-based semantic alignment and model stitching as in the cited method, with feature standardisation, zero-padding when dimensions differ, and several transformation choices. Evaluates medical-domain classification and cross-modal zero-shot classification rather than reproducing the original general-purpose experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance improves with more anchors, especially for text. Ortho performs best for text and affine for vision. Subsequent experiments use ortho with 2500 anchors.
record.code_released: Code will be available upon acceptance; no URL is stated.
record.problems: Only two models per category are used for each task except medical vision, which has one. Evaluation is limited to chest X-ray tasks. The zero-shot results are described as limited in performance, and the text does not provide the individual Figure 4 values.
record.rows_left_out: Individual point values from Figure 3 and per-model/per-task values from Figure 4 are not transcribed because the supplied text includes the figures' captions and qualitative descriptions but not their plotted values.

untested.parts: No test of whether natural image-caption alignment rises as models improve; the cross-modal map is fitted explicitly.
Relative representations, trained stitching layers, and mapping without paired anchors. The amount of loss from the cross-modal mapping is not quantified.
No feature, neuron or circuit analysis.
No variation of similarity metrics, input sets or out-of-distribution inputs; only the mapping method and anchor count vary.
No analysis of plateaus or of causes of alignment.

missing.what: Per-transformation and per-anchor-count AUROC values, and naive-stitching baseline values, for text and vision
Zero-shot comparison of general vs medical vision encoders mapped to CLIP text: general encoders outperform medical ones in most cases
Per-task zero-shot values, and the statement that zero-shot performance is limited across all models

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link and label are removed. Sensitivity to the mapping class and anchor count is a property of the V4 method, not of a similarity metric or input set, and convergence never vanishes under any choice tested. The study uses few models (two per category, one medical vision model) and chest X-ray tasks only. The cross-modal rows are method-vs-baseline comparisons, so they are not used for verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep, and no comparison of independently trained models as they become larger or more capable.
The paper aligns image and text representations for zero-shot classification, but does not test whether naturally occurring cross-modal alignment rises as both models improve.
No comparison across random initialisations of the same architecture or analysis of shared features or subspaces.
Tests anchor-based affine or orthogonal transformations and downstream stitching/classification. Does not test relative representations, layer stitching, or mapping without paired anchors.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features, neurons, circuits, or SAE features.
Tests anchor-count and transformation-method sensitivity, but not alternative similarity metrics, broad input-set variation, or out-of-distribution inputs.
Does not test whether alignment plateaus because of shared data or objectives, or whether it reflects a common model of reality.
